<div class="projects-entry-copy">

<div class="projects-entry-index">
01.1</div>

<div class="projects-entry-tags">
REGULARIZATION BY NOISE
</div>

<h3>
Can multiple noise realizations reveal information about the sample?
</h3>

<p>
Time-resolved SPAD detection preserves the arrival time of individual photons. Partitioning the photon stream into disjoint temporal windows turns a single acquisition into multiple independent Poisson realizations of the same underlying object.
</p>

<p>
In Image Scanning Microscopy, the SPAD array produces a 5×5 set of detector images, each providing a blurred observation of the same specimen. These measurements must then be combined and deconvolved to recover a higher-resolution estimate of the underlying object rather than the optically blurred image formed by the microscope.
</p>

<p>
Richardson–Lucy (RL) is a natural reconstruction method for photon-counting data because it follows the physical forward model and Poisson statistics. Its iterations are, however, semi-convergent: after an initial improvement, prolonged optimization progressively fits the measurement noise. In practice, RL therefore requires either early stopping or an explicit prior on the unknown image.
</p>

<p>
Regularization by Noise replaces morphology-based priors with agreement across independent realizations: reproducible features are preserved, while realization-specific fluctuations are suppressed. The prior is therefore statistical rather than morphological, allowing the same regularization principle to be applied across very different biological structures. The resulting coupled variational problem also leads to a nontrivial optimization task, for which we are developing a dedicated algorithm with convergence guarantees.
</p>

<div class="projects-entry-links">
<a
  href="https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.09.12.751176v1"
  target="_blank"
  rel="noopener noreferrer"
>
bioRxiv preprint · DOI 10.64898/2026.09.12.751176 ↗
</a>
</div>

<div class="projects-entry-keywords">
Poisson inverse problems · morphology-agnostic regularization · variational modelling · numerical optimization · convergence analysis
</div>

</div>


</article>

<div class="projects-entry-copy">

<div class="projects-entry-index">
01.2 · ONGOING</div>

<div class="projects-entry-tags">
PSF DISTILLER & BLIND DECONVOLUTION
</div>

<h3>
Can the microscope response be recovered directly from the data?
</h3>

<p>
The point-spread function (PSF) describes the optical response of the microscope. Aberrations distort its shape, so recovering the PSF also reveals how the imaging system departs from the ideal model.
</p>

<div class="projects-entry-subhead">CALIBRATION FROM A BEAD</div>
<p>
A fluorescent bead provides a known calibration object. In ISM, the 5×5 detector array produces 25 related PSFs whose shifts depend on detector position but whose optical content comes from the same excitation and emission paths. I fit the complete PSF grid with a physics-based model and express the recovered wavefront distortions through Zernike coefficients. On simulated data, the estimated excitation and emission coefficients can be compared directly with the ground truth.
</p>

<div class="projects-entry-subhead">BLIND DECONVOLUTION</div>
<p>
With a biological sample, the object is no longer known: the 25 detector images are blurred by PSFs that are themselves unknown. I therefore treat reconstruction as a blind multi-image inverse problem, jointly estimating the specimen and the microscope response from the same ISM acquisition while exploiting the shared image-formation physics across detector channels.
</p>

<div class="projects-entry-keywords">
Point-spread function · optical aberrations · Zernike polynomials · microscope calibration · blind deconvolution
</div>

</div>

</article>

<div class="projects-entry-copy">

<div class="projects-entry-index">
01.3</div>

<div class="projects-entry-tags">
LIFETIME UNMIXING · MODEL-BASED OPTIMIZATION
</div>

<h3>
Can reconstruction and lifetime unmixing be solved as a single inverse problem?
</h3>

<p>
Time-resolved microscopy acquires an <em>x–y–t</em> dataset: TCSPC — Time-Correlated Single-Photon Counting — adds photon-arrival time to the spatial measurement. When fluorophores overlap spectrally, differences in their fluorescence decay provide an additional contrast mechanism for multi-label separation.
</p>

<div class="projects-entry-subhead">APPROACH 1 · JOINT OPTIMIZATION</div>
<p>
In time-resolved Image Scanning Microscopy, I formulate spatial reconstruction and temporal unmixing as one spatio-temporal inverse problem, rather than reconstructing space and analysing time in separate steps.
</p>

<p>
Reference decay signatures are used to separate the mixed signal while the detector-array information recovers spatial detail. The output is therefore one separated, super-resolved reconstruction for each molecular target rather than a pixel-wise lifetime map.
</p>

<div class="projects-entry-keywords">
Spatio-temporal inverse problems · TCSPC · fluorescence lifetime · multi-target imaging · super-resolution
</div>

</div>

<section class="projects-theme-section projects-theme-white" id="learning">

<div class="projects-theme-header">

<div>

<div class="section-overline">
PHYSICS-AWARE LEARNING
</div>

<h2>
Embedding measurement physics into learning.
</h2>

</div>

<p>
Data-driven models learn complex relationships directly from microscopy measurements, while physical knowledge of image formation and signal structure remains part of the model design. Depending on the problem, this information enters through the architecture, the representation or the reconstruction constraints, keeping the learned solution connected to the acquisition.
</p>

</div>

<div class="projects-entry-visual">

<div class="projects-entry-copy">

<div class="projects-entry-index">
02.1</div>

<div class="projects-entry-tags">
LIFETIME UNMIXING · EXPLAINABLE-BY-DESIGN LEARNING
</div>

<h3>
Can the same unmixing problem be learned without hiding the physics?
</h3>

<p>
A second route is to learn the separation directly from time-resolved data. The network receives the complete <em>W × H × T</em> sequence and processes spatial and temporal information together, rather than fitting each pixel independently.
</p>

<p>
The architecture is explainable by design: separate branches predict a spatial component A<sub>i</sub> and a fluorescence-decay parameter τ<sub>i</sub> for each species. A deterministic part then rebuilds the corresponding time-resolved components and sums them back to the measured sequence, keeping the physical meaning of the intermediate outputs explicit.
</p>

<p>
Because training is constrained through reconstruction of the input sequence, the method does not require a ground-truth decomposition for every measurement. The original two-component formulation was subsequently extended toward the separation of up to four spectrally overlapping fluorophores.
</p>

<div class="projects-entry-keywords">
Fluorescence lifetime · explainable-by-design · physics-aware learning · spectral unmixing · spatio-temporal imaging
</div>

</div>

</article>

<div class="projects-entry-index">
02.2</div>

<div class="projects-entry-tags">
SINGLE-MOLECULE LOCALIZATION MICROSCOPY · SCATTERING NETWORKS · SVD
</div>

<h3>
Separating background from the signal needed for molecular localization.
</h3>

<p>
Single-molecule localization microscopy relies on detecting sparse emitter
signals in measurements that may contain substantial structured background.
Removing that background without destroying the information used for
localization is therefore part of the measurement problem itself.
</p>

<p>
In this work I explored representations based on scattering transforms
combined with singular-value decomposition to identify and separate
background structure from the signal of interest.
</p>

<p class="projects-entry-note">
The project sits between signal representation, dimensionality reduction
and computational microscopy, with the downstream localization problem
determining what information must be preserved.
</p>

</div>

<div class="section-overline">
BAYESIAN INFERENCE
</div>

<h2>
Recovering latent quantities together with uncertainty.
</h2>

</div>

<p>
Probabilistic models connect noisy measurements to hidden parameters or dynamical states. Prior information, model uncertainty and sequential updates can therefore become part of the inference rather than being treated as separate steps.
</p>

</div>

<div class="projects-entry-copy">

<div class="projects-entry-index">
03.1</div>

<div class="projects-entry-tags">
FLUORESCENCE CORRELATION SPECTROSCOPY · BAYESIAN INFERENCE · MODEL SELECTION
</div>

<h3>
Inferring how many dynamical components are hidden in a correlation measurement.
</h3>

<p>
Fluorescence correlation spectroscopy encodes molecular dynamics in the
temporal fluctuations of a detected fluorescence signal. Interpreting the
result requires inferring the dynamical components responsible for the
observed correlation function.
</p>

<p>
I worked on a Bayesian formulation in which the number of molecular species,
their diffusion times and their relative fractions are treated as unknown
quantities to be inferred from the measurement.
</p>

<p class="projects-entry-note">
The probabilistic formulation makes model uncertainty part of the inference
problem instead of fixing the number of components in advance.
</p>

</div>


</article>

<article class="projects-entry projects-entry-compact" id="bayesian-smlm">


<div class="projects-entry-copy projects-entry-copy-wide">

<div class="projects-entry-index">
03.2 · EARLY WORK</div>

<div class="projects-entry-tags">
BAYESIAN LOCALIZATION · PHOTON-LIMITED MEASUREMENTS · UNCERTAINTY
</div>

<h3>
Localization as a probabilistic inference problem.
</h3>

<p>
I also explored Bayesian formulations of localization from photon-limited
measurements, where the unknown position is inferred through a posterior
distribution rather than represented only by a single point estimate.
</p>

<p class="projects-entry-note">
This was an early-stage line of work and is presented here as part of the
broader progression toward probabilistic parameter estimation in
computational microscopy.
</p>

</div>

<div class="projects-entry-copy">

<div class="projects-entry-index">
03.3 · ONGOING</div>

<div class="projects-entry-tags">
PARTICLE TRACKING · KALMAN FILTERING · SPAD ARRAYS · FEEDBACK
</div>

<h3>
Can the microscope use the current estimate to decide what to measure next?
</h3>

<p>
Tracking a moving fluorescent particle is a sequential estimation problem.
Each acquisition contains information about the current particle position,
while the particle dynamics provide information about how that position is
expected to evolve over time.
</p>

<p>
In ongoing work extending a SPAD-based tracking framework, I combine a
dynamical model of Brownian motion with the photon-counting measurement
process in a recursive state-estimation scheme.
</p>

<p>
The estimate can then be fed back to the microscope, allowing acquisition
and inference to become parts of the same loop rather than two consecutive
stages.
</p>

<p class="projects-entry-note projects-entry-note-accent">
The estimate is not only an output of the experiment. It can become an input
to the next measurement.
</p>

</div>

<p>
Before focusing on computational microscopy, I worked on inverse problems arising from electromagnetic measurements of brain activity. The physical system was different, but the relationship between measurement design and inference was already central.

04.1</div>

<div class="projects-entry-tags">
MEG · SENSOR-ARRAY DESIGN · INVERSE SOURCE LOCALIZATION
</div>

<h3>
How should sensors be placed to make an inverse problem more informative?
</h3>

<p>
In magnetoencephalography, neuronal activity is observed indirectly through
the magnetic fields measured outside the head. The geometry and density of
the sensor array therefore influence which spatial information can be
captured and subsequently reconstructed.
</p>

<p>
My earlier work studied the design of MEG sensor arrays from this
perspective, linking spatial sampling and measurement configuration to the
inverse source-localization problem.
</p>

<p class="projects-entry-note">
This work established an early connection between two questions that remain
central in my research: what information does a measurement contain, and
how does measurement design affect what can ultimately be inferred?
</p>

</div>


</article>

<div class="projects-final-closing">

<div class="projects-final-closing-title">
Different measurements.<br>
Same mathematical habit.
</div>

<p>
Across optical imaging, photon-counting systems and electromagnetic
measurements, I am interested in the same underlying structure: identify the
quantity that matters, understand how the instrument encodes it, formulate
the resulting inference problem, and exploit that structure computationally.
</p>
